Download results

Target: 1.5× to 2× faster than the latest croc. Not achieved yet. This page records the measured iterations. Follow Prof #63.

Hardware constraint: the current 100 Mb/s LAN caps even an ideal gain at about 1.22× for the measured random workload. Inspect the line-rate bound.

Browser paths
64 MiB random input, seven isolated trials per direction. Pages preload outside timing. Completion includes saving the download and flushing the output. CD browser paths are compared with native croc on the same PC, payload size and RAM output. Croc has no browser interface in this comparison.
PathCD, msFastest native croc, mscroc / CDVerified
A ratio below 1 means CD takes longer. Direct allowed can finish on relay before ICE opens. Actual paths and byte counts are in final-browser.json. All six paths miss the 1.5× target.
Compression iteration
CD before and after disabling WebSocket compression, seven verified trials per path on a direct local workerd runtime. Both suites use the same frontend, CLI binary and Worker bundle. The handshake must match the requested setting. This is an iteration comparison, not the final croc acceptance run. The PR configuration changes; production CD has not been deployed.
PathCompression on, msCompression off, msBefore / afterVerified
Receiver completion plus flush. WebRTC carries encrypted records directly after connection; relay compression can therefore have little effect on direct paths. Wrangler's extra development proxy can negotiate compression independently, so this experiment uses a direct runtime.
File-read iteration
Browser senders now read 4 MiB source blocks while retaining 256 KiB relay frames. Seven trials per affected relay path, with compression disabled in both suites. Diagnostic instrumentation confirms 16 file reads instead of 256 for 64 MiB; those instrumented runs are excluded from the speed comparison.
PathBefore, msAfter, msBefore / after
The additional source buffer is bounded at 4 MiB. Negotiated record sizes and encrypted framing stay unchanged. Fourteen direct-allowed candidate transfers and all ten transport checks also passed; they do not constitute a new paired direct speed comparison.
Rejected experiments
These experiments did not establish a useful gain. The production storage and relay implementations remain unchanged from the retained iterations above. Complete candidate patches and verified trial data are downloadable below.
ExperimentBaseline, msCandidate, msBaseline / candidate
OPFS rows measure complete browser transfers. The relay row is a raw transport diagnostic. A separate WebRTC message-size diagnostic uses two peers in one page, so it is not a product comparison and supports no production speed claim.
Direct transport check
Raw 64 MiB WebRTC across separate browser contexts took about 2.7 seconds, reproducing much of the complete direct-transfer delay. The earlier same-page diagnostic was faster and was not an adequate match for the product layout. Route metadata confirms UDP host or peer-reflexive candidates; IP addresses are omitted.
Larger negotiated messages plus aligned encrypted records appeared faster in sequential cohorts. An alternating seven-round before/after comparison removed the apparent gain, so the framing extension was rejected.
Paired browser-to-browser directMedian, ms
Physical LAN target needs a faster link
The Linux box reports a 100 Mb/s full-duplex link. Its adapter and link partner advertise only 10/100 modes. For this 128 MiB random workload, the ideal line-rate time already exceeds the duration required to beat measured croc by 1.5×. The ideal bound ignores all protocol, encryption, launch and storage overhead.
Physical LAN timingMilliseconds
A gigabit-capable adapter and network port are needed to make the current physical-LAN target feasible. The overall goal remains unmet.
Which is faster?
The performance target is open across all required paths. Browser timings are recorded separately so interface overhead is visible alongside native transfer times.
Every answer belongs to its selected workload and route. The installed croc 10.7.0 baseline is downloadable, but the main comparison uses the verified 11.5.5 release.
Why speed changes
CD's TCP lane sends encrypted records over a native socket. WebRTC uses Pion SCTP over DTLS. The same-binary diagnostic disables TCP to measure that transport difference. Source explains the mechanisms; it does not assign CPU percentages.
The original raw browser WebSocket test took about 1.6–2.0 seconds for 64 MiB without CD encryption or disk writes. Later handshake evidence identified negotiated compression as a large part of this cost. Disabling it in a direct runtime reduced the raw test to about 0.31–0.33 seconds. The complete encrypted comparison above includes the remaining application and storage costs. A separate 16 MiB bounded HTTP echo was slower than WebSocket echo; its different buffering prevents a protocol-only conclusion. Both diagnostics are downloadable below.
croc compression is a separate variable. Both default and --no-compress are shown, including where the latter wins. Disk versus RAM also changes flush costs, so neither is silently substituted for the other.


Method and limits
The loopback matrix has 7 interleaved trials per tool and case. Each suite uses identical input bytes, warm input cache, fresh output directories and SHA-256 verification after timing. File and directory fsync are added to both tools before durable completion. Native receiver exit and sender readiness remain separate. No privileged cache dropping or host isolation.
Local CD Worker and croc relays run on the PC. Worker control storage stays in RAM for both output-storage suites. Auto allows direct discovery; the CD route evidence below each result records what actually happened. Croc's textual discovery messages do not prove its actual direct route. Forced relay disables local discovery.
The completed physical LAN suite sends 128 MiB of random bytes from this PC to Ubuntu at 192.168.1.8. Identical binaries run at both ends. CD uses a reverse SSH tunnel only for local Worker rendezvous; croc uses a private relay on the receiver machine with local discovery disabled. Bulk traffic crosses the LAN once, but rendezvous differs. LAN timing includes SSH receiver launch. RAM output is not physical persistence.
The main chart covers CLI tests; the browser table covers all three browser directions. These tests do not measure Android, public internet relay, packet-loss, directory-tree or concurrent-transfer performance. CD's numeric share code and croc's PAKE have different security properties; equal elapsed time is not evidence of equal security.
PC: 13th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i5-13420H, 12 logical CPUs, Linux 7.2.8-9-omarchy. CD was built from committed snapshot 806bb37 in a separate checkout. This acceptance run uses the retained 4 MiB browser reads and disables WebSocket compression. A direct local workerd runtime removes Wrangler’s additional development proxy. Both CLI and browser suites use that same Worker bundle. Earlier isolated results remain linked as historical evidence. The competing task was stopped before this serial acceptance run. Each data file records its own measurement time. The binary hash identifies the tested snapshot.
